CHAPTER 4.2 · LEARNING AREA 4

CHAPTER 4.2 · LEARNING AREA 4 · MAY

Conditional probability and Bayes

A rapid test is positive. How likely are you really to be ill? The answer is often surprisingly small, and to understand it you have to keep two things apart: the probability of a positive result given that you are ill and the probability of being ill given a positive result. With Bayes’ theorem you turn a tree diagram round, and with the notion of independence you check whether two characteristics have anything to do with each other at all.

8 LESSONS3 UNITS2 PRACTICE PAGESBAYES
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • to define conditional probabilities, read them off a tree and a two-way table and tell $P_A(B)$ from $P_B(A)$
  • to derive and apply the law of total probability and Bayes’ theorem, also with natural frequencies
  • to invert a tree diagram and to interpret test results critically
  • to check and justify the stochastic independence of events and of random variables

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Conditional probability

Of 200 students, 90 go by bus, that is $45\%$. But of the 80 who live outside the town, it is 60, that is $75\%$. The extra information “lives outside” turns the 200 into a smaller basic set of 80. The probability calculated within it is called conditional.

KEY POINT · CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY

For $P(A) > 0$, $P_A(B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}$ is called the probability of $B$ given $A$ (also written $P(B \mid A)$).

Multiplication rule: $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P_A(B)$. This is the 1st path rule: the branches of the second stage carry conditional probabilities.

Two-way table: $P_A(B)$ is the cell $A \cap B$ divided by the row sum $P(A)$; $P_B(A)$ is the same cell divided by the column sum $P(B)$.

Under a fixed condition all the rules still hold, for example $P_A(B) + P_A(\overline{B}) = 1$.

Do not mix them up: $P_{\text{ill}}(\text{positive})$ describes the test, $P_{\text{positive}}(\text{ill})$ is what the person tested wants to know. The two can be very different.

Laplace with a condition: with equally likely outcomes $P_A(B) = \tfrac{|A \cap B|}{|A|}$: you only count within $A$.

The Monty Hall problem: first posed in 1975 by Steve Selvin in the journal The American Statistician, made famous by Marilyn vos Savant’s column in Parade of 9 September 1990. Thousands of readers’ letters thought her correct answer was wrong.

INTERACTIVE · THE MONTY HALL PROBLEM

Choose a door. The host knows where the car is and opens another door with a goat. Do you stay or switch? Then let the computer play a thousand times.

EXAMPLE 1 · ROW AND COLUMN

Two-way table from chapter 4.1, example 4: $A$ lives outside, $B$ goes by bus; $|A \cap B| = 60$, $|A| = 80$, $|B| = 90$, $|\overline{A} \cap B| = 30$, $|\overline{A}| = 120$ out of 200. Calculate $P_A(B)$, $P_B(A)$ and $P_{\overline{A}}(B)$.

$P_A(B) = \tfrac{60}{80} = 0.75$ (row $A$), $P_B(A) = \tfrac{60}{90} \approx 0.667$ (column $B$), $P_{\overline{A}}(B) = \tfrac{30}{120} = 0.25$.

Those who live outside go by bus three times as often as the others.

EXAMPLE 2 · A DOUBLE UNDER A CONDITION

Two dice show a total of 8. How likely is a double? Conversely, how likely is the total 8 if you know that a double has been rolled?

Total 8: $(2, 6), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 3), (6, 2)$. Among them one double: $P_{\text{total 8}}(\text{double}) = \tfrac15$.

Of the 6 doubles only $(4, 4)$ has the total 8: $P_{\text{double}}(\text{total 8}) = \tfrac16$. Swapping condition and event changes the result.

EXERCISES

We have $P(A) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$. Calculate $P_A(B)$ and $P_A(\overline{B})$.

$P_A(B) = \tfrac{0.1}{0.4} = 0.25$ and $P_A(\overline{B}) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75$.

Two balls are drawn without replacement from an urn with 4 red and 6 white balls. Give the conditional probability “second red, given first red” and calculate $P(\text{both red})$.

$P_{R_1}(R_2) = \tfrac39 = \tfrac13$, so $P(R_1 \cap R_2) = \tfrac{4}{10} \cdot \tfrac13 = \tfrac{2}{15}$.

Solve the exploration “At least one head” with the definition. Why is the answer not $\tfrac12$?

$A$: at least one head $= \{HH, HT, TH\}$ with $P(A) = \tfrac34$; $P(A \cap \{HH\}) = \tfrac14$. So $P_A(HH) = \tfrac{1/4}{3/4} = \tfrac13$. $\tfrac12$ would be right if you knew that one particular coin shows heads.

In a survey $60\%$ use a streaming service ($S$), $45\%$ listen to podcasts ($Q$), $30\%$ do both. Calculate $P_S(Q)$, $P_Q(S)$ and $P_{\overline{S}}(Q)$ and interpret the result.

$P_S(Q) = \tfrac{0.3}{0.6} = 0.5$, $P_Q(S) = \tfrac{0.3}{0.45} = \tfrac23$, $P_{\overline{S}}(Q) = \tfrac{0.15}{0.4} = 0.375$. Those who stream are more likely to listen to podcasts than those who do not.

Prove: for $P(A) > 0$, $P_A(B) + P_A(\overline{B}) = 1$. Also show that $P_A$ itself satisfies Kolmogorov’s three axioms if you only consider events within $A$.

$A \cap B$ and $A \cap \overline{B}$ are mutually exclusive with union $A$, so $P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap \overline{B}) = P(A)$; divide by $P(A)$. (K1): a quotient of non-negative numbers. (K2): $P_A(A) = 1$. (K3): for mutually exclusive $B$, $C$, the events $A \cap B$ and $A \cap C$ are mutually exclusive too; the sum carries over to the quotient.

TEST YOURSELF!

$P(A) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. What is $P_A(B)$?

$\tfrac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$

A dice shows an even number. How likely is it to be a 6?

Basic set $\{2, 4, 6\}$: $\tfrac13$

$P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$. What is $P_B(A)$?

$\tfrac{0.1}{0.4} = 0.25$

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Bayes’ theorem

A rapid test detects $95\%$ of those who are ill and wrongly reacts in $5\%$ of the healthy; $2\%$ of the people tested are ill. So $P(D)$, $P_D(+)$ and $P_{\overline{D}}(+)$ are known. But the person tested wants to know $P_+(D)$. For that the tree has to be turned round: first the test result, then ill or healthy.

KEY POINT · TOTAL PROBABILITY AND BAYES’ THEOREM

Total probability: $P(B) = P(A) \cdot P_A(B) + P(\overline{A}) \cdot P_{\overline{A}}(B)$, the sum of the two paths that end in $B$.

Bayes’ theorem: $P_B(A) = \dfrac{P(A) \cdot P_A(B)}{P(A) \cdot P_A(B) + P(\overline{A}) \cdot P_{\overline{A}}(B)}$.

Inverted tree: the four path probabilities $P(A \cap B), \ldots$ stay the same. First stage $P(B)$ and $P(\overline{B})$, second stage the conditional probabilities $P_B(A) = \tfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$ and so on.

Natural frequencies: if you work with 10,000 people instead of percentages, the theorem turns into counting: positive ill people divided by all positives.

The base rate counts: if a disease is rare, there are far more healthy than ill people. Then most positive results come from healthy people, even with a good test.

Doctors put to the test: Gerd Gigerenzer gave 160 gynaecologists such a task about mammography. The most frequent answer was $90\%$, correct is about $10\%$. With natural frequencies the most frequent answer was exactly right. Source: G. Gigerenzer et al.: “Helping Doctors and Patients Make Sense of Health Statistics”, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 8 (2007), pp. 53–96.

INTERACTIVE · TURNING THE TREE ROUND

The first tree shows “first $A$, then $B$”, the second the same chance experiment the other way round: “first $B$, then $A$”. The two-way table links both. Change the three probabilities or choose an example.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE RAPID TEST

$P(D) = 0.02$, $P_D(+) = 0.95$, $P_{\overline{D}}(+) = 0.05$. Calculate $P_+(D)$ with Bayes’ theorem and with 10,000 people.

$P(+) = 0.02 \cdot 0.95 + 0.98 \cdot 0.05 = 0.019 + 0.049 = 0.068$, so $P_+(D) = \tfrac{0.019}{0.068} \approx 0.279$.

With 10,000 people: 200 ill, 190 of them positive; 9800 healthy, 490 of them positive. Of 680 positives only 190 are ill, about $28\%$.

EXAMPLE 4 · TWO MACHINES

Machine 1 makes $60\%$ of the parts with $3\%$ rejects, machine 2 the rest with $6\%$ rejects. A part is defective. Which machine is it more likely to come from?

$P(D) = 0.6 \cdot 0.03 + 0.4 \cdot 0.06 = 0.018 + 0.024 = 0.042$.

$P_D(M_1) = \tfrac{0.018}{0.042} = \tfrac37 \approx 0.43$. The defective part more likely comes from machine 2 ($\tfrac47 \approx 0.57$), although machine 2 produces less.

EXERCISES

Urn $U_1$ contains 3 red and 1 blue ball, urn $U_2$ 1 red and 3 blue. A coin chooses the urn, then a ball is drawn. Calculate $P(\text{red})$ and $P_{\text{red}}(U_1)$.

$P(\text{red}) = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac34 + \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac12$ and $P_{\text{red}}(U_1) = \tfrac{3/8}{1/2} = \tfrac34$.

Solve the exploration “The positive test”: $1\%$ ill, the test detects $90\%$ of the ill and is positive in $9\%$ of the healthy. Calculate $P_+(D)$.

$P(+) = 0.01 \cdot 0.9 + 0.99 \cdot 0.09 = 0.009 + 0.0891 = 0.0981$, so $P_+(D) = \tfrac{0.009}{0.0981} \approx 0.092$. Of 1000 people: 9 positive ill people, about 89 positive healthy people.

The person who tested positive in the previous exercise takes a second, independent test of the same kind, which is positive again. How likely is the person to be ill now?

New starting probability $P(D) \approx 0.0917$. Then $P_+(D) = \tfrac{0.0917 \cdot 0.9}{0.0917 \cdot 0.9 + 0.9083 \cdot 0.09} \approx \tfrac{0.0826}{0.1643} \approx 0.50$. Bayes can be repeated: today’s result is tomorrow’s starting probability.

A spam filter knows: $30\%$ of e-mails are spam. The word “free” appears in $40\%$ of spam e-mails and in $1\%$ of the others. An e-mail contains “free”. How likely is it to be spam?

$P(F) = 0.3 \cdot 0.4 + 0.7 \cdot 0.01 = 0.12 + 0.007 = 0.127$, so $P_F(S) = \tfrac{0.12}{0.127} \approx 0.945$.

Prove Bayes’ theorem from the definition of conditional probability and the multiplication rule.

$P_B(A) = \tfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$. In the numerator $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P_A(B)$. In the denominator $B$ splits into the mutually exclusive parts $A \cap B$ and $\overline{A} \cap B$, so $P(B) = P(A) \cdot P_A(B) + P(\overline{A}) \cdot P_{\overline{A}}(B)$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$P(A) = 0.1$, $P_A(B) = 0.8$, $P_{\overline{A}}(B) = 0.2$. What is $P(B)$?

$0.08 + 0.9 \cdot 0.2 = 0.26$

With the same numbers: what is $P_B(A)$ (three decimal places)?

$\tfrac{0.08}{0.26} \approx 0.308$

Machine 1 makes $70\%$ of the parts with $2\%$ rejects, machine 2 the rest with $5\%$. How likely does a defective part come from machine 2?

$\tfrac{0.3 \cdot 0.05}{0.7 \cdot 0.02 + 0.3 \cdot 0.05} = \tfrac{0.015}{0.029} \approx 0.517$

UNIT 32 LESSONS

3Stochastic independence

With a dice $P(H) = P(\text{at least 4}) = \tfrac12$. If you know that an even number has come up, 4 and 6 remain of 2, 4, 6: $P_E(H) = \tfrac23$. Knowing about $E$ changes the chance of $H$. For $L = \{1, 2\}$, on the other hand, $P(L) = \tfrac13$ and $P_E(L) = \tfrac13$. Here $E$ tells you nothing about $L$: the two events are independent.

KEY POINT · INDEPENDENCE

Two events $A$ and $B$ are called stochastically independent if $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$. For $P(A) > 0$ this is equivalent to $P_A(B) = P(B)$.

If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then so are $A$ and $\overline{B}$, $\overline{A}$ and $B$, and $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{B}$.

Two random variables $X$ and $Y$ are called independent if $P(X = x \text{ and } Y = y) = P(X = x) \cdot P(Y = y)$ holds for all values $x$ and $y$.

For independent random variables $E(X \cdot Y) = E(X) \cdot E(Y)$ and $V(X + Y) = V(X) + V(Y)$. Chapter 4.3 uses this for the binomial distribution.

Independent is not mutually exclusive: mutually exclusive events with $P(A), P(B) > 0$ are always dependent, because $P(A \cap B) = 0 \neq P(A) \cdot P(B)$. If you know that $A$ has occurred, you know for sure: $B$ has not.

In the tree: independent means that the second stage after $A$ and after $\overline{A}$ carries the same probabilities.

Modelling assumption: rolls of a dice or draws with replacement are assumed to be independent. In real data you have to check it, and small deviations are normal there.

INTERACTIVE · INDEPENDENT OR NOT?

Set $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A \cap B)$. The two-way table and the unit square show when $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$ holds.

EXAMPLE 5 · CHECKING A TWO-WAY TABLE

Of 200 people, 50 wear glasses ($G$), 20 are left-handed ($L$), 5 both. Are “glasses” and “left-handed” independent in this group?

$P(G \cap L) = \tfrac{5}{200} = 0.025$ and $P(G) \cdot P(L) = 0.25 \cdot 0.1 = 0.025$.

Equal, so independent: among those who wear glasses the proportion of left-handers, $\tfrac{5}{50} = 10\%$, is just as large as overall.

EXAMPLE 6 · INDEPENDENT RANDOM VARIABLES

Two coins are tossed. $X_1$ and $X_2$ count the heads of the first and of the second coin, $Y = X_1 + X_2$. Are $X_1$ and $X_2$ independent? And $X_1$ and $Y$?

For all four pairs $(a, b)$, $P(X_1 = a, X_2 = b) = \tfrac14 = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12$: independent.

But $P(X_1 = 1, Y = 0) = 0$, while $P(X_1 = 1) \cdot P(Y = 0) = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac18$. $X_1$ and $Y$ are dependent: the sum contains the first coin.

EXERCISES

We have $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.15$. Are $A$ and $B$ independent?

Yes, $0.5 \cdot 0.3 = 0.15$.

Two components fail independently of each other; they work with probabilities $0.95$ and $0.9$. How reliable is a series circuit (both needed) and a parallel circuit (one is enough)?

Series: $0.95 \cdot 0.9 = 0.855$. Parallel: $1 - 0.05 \cdot 0.1 = 0.995$.

Prove: if $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $A$ and $\overline{B}$ are independent too.

$P(A \cap \overline{B}) = P(A) - P(A \cap B) = P(A) - P(A) \cdot P(B) = P(A)\,\big(1 - P(B)\big) = P(A) \cdot P(\overline{B})$.

A dice is rolled twice. $X$ is the first score, $Y$ the total. Show that $X$ and $Y$ are dependent.

$P(X = 1, Y = 12) = 0$, but $P(X = 1) \cdot P(Y = 12) = \tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac{1}{36} \neq 0$. A single counterexample is enough.

Two coins: $A$ “first shows heads”, $B$ “second shows heads”, $C$ “both show the same”. Show: any two of the three events are independent, but $P(A \cap B \cap C) \neq P(A) \cdot P(B) \cdot P(C)$.

All three have the probability $\tfrac12$, and every pairwise intersection is $\{HH\}$: $P(A \cap B) = P(A \cap C) = P(B \cap C) = \tfrac14 = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12$. But $A \cap B \cap C = \{HH\}$ also has $\tfrac14 \neq \tfrac18$. So pairwise independent does not yet mean that all three together are independent.

TEST YOURSELF!

$A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A) = 0.4$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. What is $P(A \cap B)$?

$0.4 \cdot 0.5 = 0.2$

$A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.6$. What is $P(A \cup B)$?

$0.3 + 0.6 - 0.18 = 0.72$

$P(A) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$. For which $P(B)$ are $A$ and $B$ independent?

$0.4 \cdot P(B) = 0.1$, so $P(B) = 0.25$.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A burglar alarm goes off with $99\%$ in the case of a burglary, and with $0.5\%$ on a night without a burglary. The probability of a burglary on a given night is $0.01\%$. The alarm goes off. How likely is a burglary?

$\dfrac{0.0001 \cdot 0.99}{0.0001 \cdot 0.99 + 0.9999 \cdot 0.005} = \dfrac{0.000099}{0.0050985} \approx 0.019$. Almost every alarm is a false alarm, because burglaries are so rare.

Solve the Monty Hall problem with Bayes’ theorem: you choose door 1, the host opens door 3 with a goat. He chooses at random if he has two goat doors to choose from. How likely is the car behind door 2?

$A_i$: car behind door $i$, $\tfrac13$ each. $M_3$: the host opens door 3. $P_{A_1}(M_3) = \tfrac12$, $P_{A_2}(M_3) = 1$, $P_{A_3}(M_3) = 0$, so $P(M_3) = \tfrac16 + \tfrac13 = \tfrac12$. $P_{M_3}(A_2) = \tfrac{1/3}{1/2} = \tfrac23$: switching doubles the chance of winning.

Two dice: $X$ and $Y$ are the scores. Confirm $E(X \cdot Y) = E(X) \cdot E(Y)$ by calculation and explain why this does not hold for $X$ and $X$.

$E(X \cdot Y) = \tfrac{1}{36}\sum_{x, y} x y = \tfrac{1}{36} \cdot 21 \cdot 21 = 12.25 = 3.5^2$. For $X \cdot X$: $E(X^2) = \tfrac{91}{6} \approx 15.17 \neq 12.25$, because $X$ is not independent of itself.

In a two-way table $P(A) = 0.5$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. In which range can $P(A \cap B)$ lie? For which value are $A$ and $B$ independent?

All cells are at least 0: $P(A \cap B) \le 0.4$, and $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 1 - 0.9 + P(A \cap B) \ge 0$ always holds. So $0 \le P(A \cap B) \le 0.4$; independent for $0.2$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

A theorem from the papers he left behind

Thomas Bayes was a minister in Tunbridge Wells in England and died in April 1761. He never published his famous idea. Among his papers his friend Richard Price found an essay, edited it, wrote an introduction and an appendix and presented it to the Royal Society in London in December 1763.

Bayes asked the question that nobody had answered cleanly until then: you only observe the effects, for instance how often an event occurs. What can be said from this about the unknown cause, about the probability itself? He thought of balls rolling onto a table and calculated back from the result. This “inverse probability” is exactly the turning round of the tree from unit 2.

Independently of him, Pierre-Simon Laplace arrived at the same idea a few years later and made it widely known. Today the theorem is at work in spam filters, in medical diagnosis and in machine learning.

Source: Thomas Bayes, Richard Price: “An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances”, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 53 (1763), pp. 370–418.

Work it out: with the numbers of the rapid test from example 3, a second, independent positive test raises the probability of being ill from about $28\%$ to about $88\%$.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY

$P_A(B) = \tfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}$; in the table, cell divided by the row or column sum.

Bus given “outside”: $\tfrac{60}{80} = 0.75$

MULTIPLICATION RULE

$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P_A(B)$: the 1st path rule.

Two red without replacement: $\tfrac{4}{10} \cdot \tfrac39$

TOTAL PROBABILITY

$P(B) = P(A)\,P_A(B) + P(\overline{A})\,P_{\overline{A}}(B)$.

Positive: $0.019 + 0.049 = 0.068$

BAYES’ THEOREM

$P_B(A) = \tfrac{P(A)\,P_A(B)}{P(B)}$; inverted tree, natural frequencies.

$P_+(D) \approx 0.279$: 190 of 680 positives

INDEPENDENCE

$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$; random variables: for all pairs of values.

Even and at most 2: $\tfrac16 = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac13$
